opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the more interesting and genuinely uncertain questions coming out of our work. The headline result from the original paper was that the length of tasks AI agents can complete with 50% reliability has been doubling roughly every seven months, going back to around 2019. But when you look at just the more recent models, from roughly 2024 onward, the doubling time looks noticeably shorter, something more like four months.

How I interpret that, though, depends a lot on being careful about what the data can and can't tell us. A few things I'd flag.

First, the recent window is short and has relatively few models in it, so the confidence intervals on that faster slope are wide. Fitting a trend to a handful of frontier releases is just much noisier than fitting to six years of data. So I wouldn't treat "four months" as a precise new constant.

Second, there are plausible substantive reasons it could be real. The recent period coincides with a shift toward reasoning models, heavy RL on agentic tasks, and a lot more effort specifically aimed at making models good at long, multi-step software work. It wouldn't be shocking if that changed the rate of progress on exactly the kind of tasks we measure.

Third, there are reasons for caution about the measurement itself. Our task suite is mostly software engineering and research-style tasks that are fairly clean and well specified, with automatic scoring. Labs may be optimizing increasingly hard for that kind of task distribution, so faster progress on our benchmark might partly reflect that rather than an equally fast increase in general capability on messier real-world work. We also have the issue that as models get better, the longer tasks in our suite get sparser, so estimates at the top end rely on fewer data points.

So my overall take is something like: I think there's real evidence that progress has sped up recently, and I'd put meaningful weight on that, but I'd hold the specific number loosely. The more important point for forecasting is that even the original seven-month trend, if it continued, implies pretty dramatic capabilities within a few years. A faster trend just pulls those dates in. Whether it continues depends on things like compute scaling, whether RL gains keep generalizing, and whether there are bottlenecks we haven't hit yet, and honestly I think it's one of the most important things to keep measuring.

r001.rationale: It says recent progress appears faster and gives a roughly four-month doubling time, but does not judge whether that trend predicts recent frontier performance better than the seven-month trend.

r002.rationale: It is skeptical because the recent window has few models and wide confidence intervals, but does not mention fitting piecewise trends or roughly 10 to 15 data points.

r003.rationale: It treats the four-month estimate cautiously, but does not characterize the trend as a faster exponential or distinguish it from established super-exponential growth.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I'm fairly uncertain about how to interpret it, and I want to be careful not to over-read a trend that's based on a pretty small number of data points at the frontier.

So just to set the stage for people: the original METR result was that the length of tasks AI systems can complete with something like fifty percent reliability, measured in terms of how long those tasks take a human expert, has been doubling roughly every seven months, going back to about 2019. And then if you look at just the last year or two, the models that have come out since early 2024, the doubling time looks more like four months. So the question is whether that's a real acceleration or whether it's noise.

I think there are a few things going on. One is that a lot of the recent gains seem to come from reinforcement learning on reasoning and agentic tasks, which is a somewhat different regime from the pretraining scaling that drove the earlier part of the curve. Labs found a new lever, and they pulled it hard, and it's plausible that you get a burst of fast progress when a new technique comes online that then settles back into a slower trend. That's happened before in ML. So I don't think we should assume the four-month number is the new steady state.

The second thing is that the benchmark itself has limitations that matter more as the horizons get longer. The tasks are software and research-flavored, they're reasonably well-specified, they have clean success criteria. The error bars on the longest tasks are big because there just aren't many of them. And there's the whole question of whether fifty percent reliability on a scaffolded, self-contained task translates into what people actually mean when they say "this AI can do a week of work." I think the answer is partly yes but it overstates things, and I worry that the acceleration partly reflects models getting better at the specific shape of these tasks rather than at open-ended work in general.

That said, I don't want to be dismissive, because the version of me from a couple years ago would have been surprised by where we are now. Even if you take the seven-month trend at face value, that's already a pretty wild claim about the next few years. And the fact that the recent points are above the line rather than below it is at least some evidence that things aren't slowing down. So my overall take is something like: I put real weight on the acceleration being partly real, I'd want to see a few more generations of models before I update my long-run forecast much, and I think the more important work right now is building evaluations that tell us whether these longer horizons hold up on messier, less well-specified tasks, because that's where the actual question about what these systems can do gets answered.

r001.rationale: The response reports a roughly four-month doubling time recently and says recent points are above the earlier trend line, but it does not clearly judge that the four-month trend predicted recent frontier performance better.

r002.rationale: It notes uncertainty from a small number of frontier data points, but does not discuss fitting piecewise trends or give the roughly 10–15-point estimate.

r003.rationale: The response is cautious about whether the faster trend will persist, but does not clearly frame it as a faster exponential rather than established super-exponential growth.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish two claims. One is that the seven-month doubling trend might underestimate how quickly capabilities are improving right now. The other is that we’ve established a new, persistently faster doubling rate. You can have evidence for the first without having very strong evidence for the second.

A time horizon is a summary of performance on a particular set of tasks, at a particular reliability threshold. So I’d want to know how sensitive the apparent acceleration is to the tasks included, the models selected, and the amount of scaffolding or inference compute they get. Those improvements can be real and useful, but they affect what we should extrapolate.

If the faster trend survives those checks, that would make me put more weight on shorter timelines for AI systems being able to carry out substantial projects autonomously. But I’d still be cautious about taking a doubling rate fitted to a short recent window and projecting it out for years. The evidence can warrant a meaningful update without warranting that kind of precision.

r001.rationale: The response says the seven-month trend may underestimate current progress, but does not say a four-month trend predicted recent frontier performance better.

r002.rationale: It cautions against extrapolating from a short recent window, but does not discuss piecewise trends or the roughly 10 to 15 data points.

r003.rationale: It treats a faster doubling rate as a plausible interpretation while stressing that a persistently faster rate is not established and that the short-window fit merits low confidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d take it as evidence that the seven-month trend isn’t a law of nature, but I’d be cautious about concluding that we’ve established a new, faster doubling time. If you fit a trend to just the most recent models, you can get a much steeper slope, and that estimate can be pretty sensitive to which models and dates you include.

There’s also a distinction between the measured time horizon and what we ultimately care about. This is roughly the duration of tasks, measured by how long they take humans, that an AI can complete at a given success rate. It’s not directly measuring how long an AI can operate autonomously in the world. The task distribution, the scaffolding, and the reliability threshold all matter.

So I think the update is toward taking faster progress seriously, including in planning. I wouldn’t confidently extrapolate the recent faster rate indefinitely. But I also wouldn’t use the original seven-month estimate as a reason to dismiss what the newer results are showing.

r001.rationale: The response says recent-model fits can show a steeper slope, but does not judge that a four-month trend predicted recent frontier performance better than the seven-month trend.

r002.rationale: It notes that a recent-model trend fit is sensitive to model and date selection, but does not specifically address piecewise trends or roughly 10 to 15 data points.

r003.rationale: It expresses caution about treating a faster doubling time as established, but does not characterize the trend as a faster exponential or distinguish it from super-exponential growth.
